data.title: Real estate shrugs off Q3 slump as investment sales hit record $47.52b
data.description:
Public-sector deals rose 51.5% while private real estate investment fell 42.5% in Q3.

Real estate investment sales fell 21.2% quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) to $12.06b in the third quarter (Q3) of 2026 following two quarters of strong performance, according to Savills Singapore.

Even with Q3’s slowdown, total investment sales in the first nine months of the year reached $47.52b, surpassing all previous full-year totals since market tracking began in 2008.

Q3 transaction value also remained 6% above the $11.38b recorded in Q3 2025.

Transaction momentum moderated in Q3 amidst global economic uncertainty, the prolonged Middle East conflict, and an unclear interest rate outlook.

Private-sector investment sales contracted sharply by 42.5% to $6.81b, weighed down by the absence of major big-ticket transactions.

Residential assets overtook commercial assets to become the largest contributor to investment sales, accounting for 40.7% of total transaction value.

Despite its leading share, residential investment sales also declined 9.9% QoQ to $4.91b, largely due to fewer residential Government Land Sales (GLS) site awards and slower home sales during the Hungry Ghost Month.

Meanwhile, commercial investment sales fell to $2.02b from $8.04b in Q2, and account for 16.7% of total sales, down from 52.5%.

In contrast, public-sector investment sales rose 51.5% to $5.26b.
The GLS sites at Bayshore Drive ($2.13b) and the GLS site at New Upper Changi Road ($1.43b) accounted for 67.6% of the public-sector sales this quarter.

“Whilst investment sales have reached record levels this year, the divergence between public- and private-sector activity has become more apparent,” said Alan Cheong, executive director for research and consultancy at Savills.

“Government land sales continue to support transaction volumes, but the absence of major private-sector deals suggests that investment momentum is becoming increasingly uneven,” he added.

But with the completion of major transactions uncertain, Savills expects a calmer fourth quarter for real estate investments.

data.title: Japan sublease divestments push Food Innovators to $395,000 net loss
data.description:
The decline was partially offset by gains in its food retail business.

Food Innovators Holdings Ltd (FIH) swung to a net loss of $395,000 in the first half of financial year 2027 from a net profit of $206,000 a year earlier, as lower contributions from its restaurant leasing and subleasing business (RLSB) weighed on performance.

The period ran from March to August 2026.

Revenue decreased 5.8% to $22.5m, mainly due to lower contributions from the RLSB in Japan. Revenue from the RLSB dropped 17.4% to $8.6m following the divestment of ten mature sublease properties in the previous corresponding period.

Gross profit fell 8.5% year-on-year (YoY) to $3.4m, with gross profit margin edging down 0.5 percentage points to 15.3%.

The declines were partially offset by the food retail business, where gross profit rose 32.4% YoY to $2.4m, and revenue grew 3.2% to $13.9m.

Other income fell to $234,000 from $496,000 as the previous period included a one-off government grant of approximately $300,000 for IPO-related professional fees.

FIH also posted a share of loss of about $100,000 from its joint ventures due to initial start-up costs at Yaruki Malaysia, which opened its first restaurant during the period.

The group targets two new restaurant openings in Southeast Asia for 2026 and a yakiniku restaurant in January 2027. It currently manages 235 subleased properties in Japan and operates 34 restaurants across Singapore, Japan, and Malaysia.

data.title: SID appoints Max Loh as chair amidst leadership shift
data.description:
He succeeds former PwC executive chairman Yeoh Oon Jin.

The Singapore Institute of Directors (SID) has appointed Max Loh Khum Wai as the new chair of its governing council as part of a broader leadership renewal, the company announced.

Loh takes over Yeoh Oon Jin, who stepped down after serving three years in the role.

Loh has served on SID’s governing council since 2019, bringing expertise in audit, business advisory, corporate finance, risk management, and business transformation, SID said.

He currently serves as chairman of the Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore and deputy chairman of the Building and Construction Authority.

Loh’s appointment comes as the governing council undergoes a planned leadership transition, with changes to the chair and CEO roles, SID said.

Two members, Neil Parekh and Justin Ang, have stepped down as part of the renewal, whilst Kevin Lai joined the council. Joy Tan and June Sim, who were co-opted last year, were elected to the council.

Four existing members, Max Loh, Ivan Ng, Karen Loon, and Ooi Huey Tyng, were reelected for another term.

SID said the governing council oversees the affairs of the institute and serves as its board of directors.

data.title: International visitor arrivals fall 6.6% to 3.76 million in Q2
data.description:
The average length of stay shortened by 1.5% to 3.51 days.

Singapore's international visitor arrivals declined 6.6% year-on-year (YoY) to 3.76 million in the second quarter, according to Singapore Tourism Board (STB) data.

Overnight visitors fell 9.4% to 2.69 million during the April-to-June period. Total visitor days dropped 8% to 13.17 million.

The average length of stay also shortened by 1.5% to 3.51 days.

Visitor arrivals declined YoY across all three months of the quarter.

In April, Singapore received approximately 1.33 million visitors, down 5.1% from 1.40 million a year earlier.

Arrivals fell further to 1.24 million in May, compared with 1.37 million in the same month of 2025, marking the sharpest year-on-year decline of the quarter at 9.7%. 

June recorded approximately 1.18 million arrivals, compared with 1.25 million a year earlier.

The figures were published on STB's Singapore Tourism Analytics Network, last updated on 15 October.

data.title: First Resources blames El Niño as fires reach Indonesian plantations
data.description:
Some fires started outside its operating areas and could not be fully contained. 

First Resources Limited confirmed that fires had spread into areas under its management in West Kalimantan, Indonesia, citing severe El Niño-related drought as a major factor behind heightened fire risks. 

The group said in a filing dated 15 October that prolonged dry conditions had increased the risk of fires spreading across surrounding lands and escalating into uncontrolled wildfires.

It added that plantations near concession boundaries, community-owned lands, and unmanaged areas faced higher fire risks.

"The presence of hotspots within a concession should not, in itself, be interpreted as an indication that the concession holder caused, initiated or condoned a fire," First Resources said.

Meanwhile, the group said it conducts daily satellite monitoring, drone surveillance, and ground patrols to manage fire risks.

Its firefighting teams have been stationed near plantation boundaries to support suppression efforts and coordinate with neighbouring companies.

First Resources said it had distributed 17 sets of water pump units to affected villages and provided thousands of masks to local education offices for distribution to schools.

“The group will continue working closely with relevant authorities, local communities, and other stakeholders to mitigate fire risks and support suppression efforts,” it added.

data.title: KPay secures MPI licence in Singapore
data.description:
KPay is authorised to provide domestic and cross-border money transfer services.

KPay’s subsidiary KPay Merchant Service (Singapore) Pte Ltd. has secured a major payment institution (MPI) licence by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).

With the license, KPay is authorised to provide merchant acquisition, domestic money transfer, and cross-border money transfer services.

KPay established Singapore operations in 2022 and serves over 10,000 merchants locally.

KPay said it is expanding its merchant offering across both online and in-store commerce, and is introducing online payment capabilities for e-commerce transactions, digital invoicing, and remote payment collection.

KPay is also introducing a point of sale solution for the F&B sector.

KPay operates across Australia, Hong Kong, Japan, and Singapore.

data.title: September key exports jump 68.4% on ship shipments and AI demand
data.description:
Non-electronics NODX grew 54.2% from 11.9% in August.

Non-oil domestic exports (NODX) jumped 68.4% year-on-year in September, extending August's 46.1% growth, according to Enterprise Singapore.

The expansion was driven by non-electronics, alongside continued demand for artificial intelligence (AI)-related electronics.

Non-electronics NODX expanded 54.2%, up from 11.9% in the previous month, led by structures of ships and boats, which contributed $3.7b to the increase.

Non-monetary gold and specialised machinery also contributed $1.1b and $1.0b, respectively.

Meanwhile, electronics exports rose 107.6%, moderating from 131.6% in August.

Growth was supported by disk media products (+312.4%), integrated circuits (+74.7%), and personal computers (+149.5%), contributing $1.7b, $1.5b, and $0.9b, respectively.

By market, exports to Hong Kong surged 112.1%, followed by Taiwan (+96.9%) and South Korea (+96.0%).

Exports to the US grew 73.2%, easing from 90.9%. However, shipments to India declined 5.6%, reversing the previous month's 23.6% growth.

NODX expanded 27.6% in the first nine months.

Separately, non-oil re-exports grew 47.8% in September, moderating from 53.2% in the previous month. Electronic re-exports climbed 64.2%, whilst non-electronic re-exports rose 22.1%.

Total merchandise trade expanded 50.8%, extending the 44.4% increase in August, as total exports and imports rose 51.5% and 49.9%, respectively.

data.title: New home sales double as buyers chase value
data.description:
Analysts said buyers remained selective amid price, interest-rate and employment concerns.

New private home sales nearly doubled in September as buyers returned after the Lunar Seventh Month and responded to price adjustments at existing projects.

Developers sold 296 homes excluding executive condominiums, up 93.5% from 153 units in August and 16.1% from 255 units a year earlier.

Analysts cautioned that the increase came from a low base after developers held back launches during the seasonal lull.

Realion Chief Researcher and Strategist Christine Sun said about two-thirds of September’s transactions occurred after 10 September, when the Lunar Seventh Month ended.

PropNex Head of Research and Content Wong Siew Ying said the recovery was supported mainly by previously launched projects. Apart from the 24 units sold at Amberwood at Holland, existing developments accounted for about 92% of September’s sales.

She said the figures demonstrated a steady base of demand but also showed that buyers had become more discerning about pricing, location and project attributes.

Terra Hill was the month’s best-selling project, moving 32 units at a median price of $2,209 psf. It was followed by The Sen with 25 units and Amberwood at Holland with 24.

CBRE Head of Research for Singapore and Southeast Asia Tricia Song said discounts of approximately 15% to 18% helped Terra Hill record its strongest monthly sales since its February 2023 launch. The project was about 92% sold by the end of September.

Wong said Terra Hill’s performance showed that buyers remained willing to enter the market when a project stood out on value. However, she described the price adjustments as project-specific rather than evidence of a broad change in new-home pricing.

The Rest of Central Region accounted for 131 units, or about 44% of September’s sales. The Outside Central Region contributed 125 units, whilst the Core Central Region recorded 40.

New launches received a more measured response. Amberwood at Holland sold 24 of the 70 units released during its initial phase at a median price of $3,021 psf.

Huttons Asia CEO Mark Yip said the development’s larger units appealed to families, but the higher purchase amounts limited its potential buyer pool. More than 60% of its September sales involved four- and five-bedroom units.

Huttons also highlighted the sale of 19 landed homes during the month, the highest monthly figure since April 2018.

Yip attributed the increase to wealth accumulation among Singapore households and a narrowing price premium between new and resale terrace homes.

Despite the September recovery, analysts said affordability and economic uncertainty would continue to shape demand.

Song said high price points, fewer launches, global uncertainty and interest-rate concerns had made buyers increasingly selective.

Knight Frank Singapore Head of Research Leonard Tay said higher borrowing costs, rising retrenchments and uncertainty over the employment impact of artificial intelligence could make households more cautious about taking on long-term mortgages.

Land costs could add further pressure. Knight Frank estimated that the average land rate for non-landed residential government sites increased about 21% over the latest 12-month period compared with the preceding year.

Tay said this could make projects launched in 2026 appear relatively attractive against future developments built on more expensive land.

Sales are expected to strengthen in the fourth quarter as new supply enters the market.

Lucerne Grand sold 350 of its 570 units during its launch weekend in early October, whilst the upcoming 1,268-unit Thomson Reserve will provide a broader test of buyers’ appetite and pricing limits.

Full-year projections range from 6,500 to 8,000 units. Knight Frank expects between 6,500 and 7,500 sales, CBRE forecasts 7,500 to 8,000, and Huttons projects approximately 7,000.

Analysts broadly expect the market to remain supported by household wealth and low unemployment, but said project pricing would determine whether developers can convert buyer interest into sales.

data.title: Developers cautious as Marina Gardens Lane draws one bid
data.description:
Analysts cited CBD sales risks, future housing supply over how quickly the Marina South precinct will mature.

Developers remain cautious about Marina South despite steady sales at its first private residential project, property analysts said after the latest Marina Gardens Lane government land sales site attracted only one bid.

EL Development submitted an offer of about $450.1m, equivalent to $1,243 psf per plot ratio, for the 0.6-hectare residential and commercial site.

The land rate was 11.3% below the $1,402 psf ppr paid for the neighboring site in 2023. That plot, which attracted four bids, is being developed as One Marina Gardens.

The latest site could yield approximately 390 private homes and 150 sq m of ground-floor commercial space. Its award remains pending.

CBRE Head of Research for Singapore and Southeast Asia Tricia Song said the below-expected bid reflected continued developer caution toward CBD sites.

She cited expectations of higher interest rates, weaker take-up at recent project launches and uncertain end-user demand. The 60% additional buyer’s stamp duty imposed on foreigners has also reduced foreign and investment purchases, increasing the sales risk for developers.

The lack of a primary school within 1km, limited nearby amenities and a smaller pool of upgrader buyers could also constrain demand, Song said.

Knight Frank Singapore Head of Research Leonard Tay said developers may prefer to conserve capital for established residential neighborhoods where demand from HDB upgraders and homeowners seeking smaller properties is more predictable.

Construction costs, the large future housing pipeline and uncertainty over the pace at which Marina South will mature also contributed to the subdued response.

Tay said the tender illustrated a distinction between developers’ confidence in Marina South’s long-term potential and the more conservative land prices they were currently prepared to accept.

PropNex Head of Research and Content Wong Siew Ying similarly said developers were taking a measured view of the precinct even though One Marina Gardens had recorded steady sales.

The project had sold about 672 of its 937 units, or 72%, at an average price of approximately $2,970 psf as of 4 October.

However, the opening of Marina South MRT station has been deferred until the surrounding area is further developed. Additional supply could also emerge from the nearby Marina Gardens Crescent reserve-list site, which could yield about 775 homes.

More than 10,000 private and public homes are planned in Marina South over the longer term.

Huttons Asia CEO Mark Yip said developers were becoming more selective and tightly managing liquidity amid geopolitical uncertainty, higher construction costs and interest-rate risks.

However, Huttons expects the site to be awarded because the $1,243 psf ppr offer is 26% above the $984 psf ppr bid for Marina Gardens Crescent that the government rejected in 2024 for being too low.

The lower land price could also provide EL Development with a buffer against higher development costs and market uncertainty.

Analysts said the site still offered several advantages, including proximity to the CBD, Marina Bay Financial Centre and Marina Bay Sands, as well as potential views of Gardens by the Bay and future access to Marina South MRT station.

Launch-price estimates varied. Knight Frank expects a future project to achieve an average price of between $2,700 and $2,900 psf, whilst CBRE forecasts $2,850 to $2,950 psf. PropNex expects the average price to exceed $2,900 psf.

Analysts expect developer confidence to improve as Marina South becomes more established and additional transport links, housing and amenities are completed.
